newsitem.title: PERU: Christmas carols, prayers for Peru hostages.
newsitem.headline: Christmas carols, prayers for Peru hostages.

text.p: Blonde girls in red miniskirts belted out carols through loudspeakers to 105 hostages spending Christmas under the guns of Marxist rebels inside the besieged Japanese embassy residence in Peru.

A Jesuit priest who earlier turned down his chance of freedom was to hold a candlelit midnight mass for the mainly Catholic captives, spending their eighth night as prisoners of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).

Peruvians prayed for a Christmas miracle to set the hostages free, staging marches in provincial towns and hoisting flags from their homes. Family members sent seasonal messages over the airwaves to their loved ones.
"Happy Christmas Dad, I hope you stay as strong as ever," said Eduardo Martell, the son of captive Honduran ambassador Jose Martell. "I'm sure that soon we will be hugging each other again."

"Brother, I'm sending you a huge hug ... God bless you, have faith like us, have hope that everything will end well," said Leonor Siura, the sister of captive Peruvian congressman Gilberto Siura, in a radio address.

The six mini-skirted girls, belonging to an American volunteer group called The Family, gave their impromptu concert from a scaffold erected next to police lines by the residence in the hope of cheering hostages' spirits.
Based in Peru, The Family normally performs in shanty towns and slums, handing out food to the poor, choir member Liz Alexander told Reuters.
Reinforcing the Christmas spirit, a man dressed as Santa Claus mingled with waiting journalists from around the world gathered to record the drama.
Nearby residents heeded calls from police to avoid setting off traditional Christmas fireworks so as not to alarm the heavily armed young hostage-takers.
The MRTA rebels stormed a smart reception at the residence last Tuesday night, taking prisoner about 500 VIPs from around the world.

Most -- including the old, the women, all the American and European hostages and Tuesday evening the Uruguayan ambassador -- have now been released in what the rebels described as humanitarian gestures.

But the guerrillas were holding on to all the Peruvian government officials, including President Alberto Fujimori's brother Pedro, the foreign minister and the head of the anti- terrorist police -- to press their demands for the release of jailed comrades.
Fujimori has rejected the conditions and told the guerrillas to surrender. But he also insisted in a letter to Pope John Paul made public on Tuesday that he wanted a peaceful end to the crisis.
Six ambassadors from Latin America and Asia, plus around 30 Japanese nationals, are among the hostages.
"We can't celebrate Christmas knowing they are all in there," Tania Verdeguer, a friend of one of the hostages, told Reuters as she prayed for the captives near press lines.
YMCA volunteers sent bibles for the Red Cross to take to the hostages along with Christmas meals that included traditional Japanese bento boxes -- packed lunches of fish and rice.

The hostages got a crumb of Christmas comfort when Peruvian police allowed the Red Cross to pump water into residence tanks to allow toilets to function for the first time since the mains supply was cut off last week.
Torches were also let into the residence to lessen the danger of an accident among the hostages during the nights of captivity, the Red Cross said.

Inside the residence, Jesuit priest Juan Julio Wicht was to celebrate communion for the hostages. Red Cross workers were seen delivering candles and sacraments to the grand entrance of the residence on Tuesday evening.
Wicht turned down the chance of leaving the residence along with a group of 225 men set free on Sunday night, saying he preferred to stay and tend to his flock.

But hopes of a big pre-Christmas hostage release were dashed. The only hostage set free on Christmas Eve was Uruguayan ambassador Tabare Bocalandro, released after his country liberated two MRTA prisoners.
Uruguay's Foreign Minister Alvaro Ramos officially claimed the two events were a coincidence but a well-placed government source told Reuters a deal had in fact been struck.
Speculation here continued that Cuba might be ready to offer sanctuary to the rebels in return for the safe release of all the hostages but there was no official confirmation of this.
